name: EU Space Act
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: impact assessment with cost estimates; qualitative critiques; proposal pending
summary: The Commission expects one EU-wide licensing regime for space activities to replace 13 or more national systems, reduce space debris and cyber risks, and help European start-ups grow, at the price of satellites costing 3-10% more to build. The United States and some companies argue the burden is higher and unfairly hits non-EU operators. The proposal is still under negotiation, so there is no evidence of effects yet.

indicators.objective: No LFS indicators extracted; memorandum says specific objectives would be monitored annually and the act evaluated five years after entry into force (IA executive summary says three years), focusing on market and SME impact

indicators.indicator: One set of EU licensing requirements instead of 13+ national regimes; lower administrative burden; cross-border recognition
Satellite manufacturing cost increase from binding safety, resilience and environmental requirements
indicators.target_or_baseline: +3-10% vs baseline; risk management up to EUR 240,000 initial then ~1% of turnover
indicators.evidence: Forecast only; US government and some industry argue costs and burdens are underestimated and discriminatory (qualitative, no published cost estimate).

indicators.indicator: Less space debris; trackable space objects; cybersecurity risk framework; common environmental footprint method

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Regulation on the safety, resilience and sustainability of space activities in the Union (EU Space Act), SWD(2025) 335 (executive summary SWD(2025) 336)
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Regulation on the safety, resilience and sustainability of space activities in the Union (EU Space Act)
literature.outcomes: compliance costs; single market; competitiveness; space debris
literature.headline: Preferred option (binding EU framework plus support measures): satellite manufacturing costs +3-10% vs baseline; risk management up to EUR 240,000 initially then 1% of turnover; benefits (less debris and cyber risk, business continuity, single market, attracting investment) described qualitatively
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected a single EU licensing regime to cut red tape and make space safer and greener, while raising satellite manufacturing costs by 3-10%.
literature.verified: executive summary read; full text searched

literature.citation: US Departments of State and Commerce (2025), U.S. Government feedback on the draft EU Space Act, Comments released 4 November 2025
literature.authors: US Departments of State and Commerce
literature.title: U.S. Government feedback on the draft EU Space Act
literature.method: qualitative (drawing on input from 70+ companies and trade associations)
literature.headline: Argues the act would impose unacceptable regulatory burdens and drive up costs, especially via environmental requirements, and that some provisions (e.g. on large constellations) unfairly target non-EU operators; no quantified cost estimate
literature.summary_plain: The US government said the EU Space Act would raise costs and unfairly burden American satellite operators, but gave no cost figures.
